source: Belfield, S. and Brown, C. (2010). Guidebook on Upland Crops in Cambodia: Corn (សៀវភៅណែនាំ ស្តីពីដំណាំតំបន់ខ្ពង់រាបនៅក្នុងប្រទេសកម្ពុជា៖ ដំណាំពោត). ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. Uploaded PDF, 52 pages, image-only (Limon-font-era scan, read via page rasterization).
text:
A multi-season trial (Bell et al. 2005) measured corn yield (t/ha) across seven named soil groups in Battambang/Kampong Cham, over early-wet-season (EWS) and wet-season (WS) plantings in 2004 and 2005:

- Kampong Siem: EWS2004 1.75, EWS2005 n/a, WS2004 4.09, WS2005 2.09, average 2.64
- Kroeun Snay: EWS2004 2.75, EWS2005 1.16, WS2004 2.85, WS2005 3.94, average 2.49
- Tuol Samrong: EWS2004 2.25, EWS2005 1.30, WS2004 1.87, WS2005 1.62, average 1.84
- Kampong Siem (with lime/calcareous content): EWS2004 1.05, EWS2005 2.52, WS2004 1.40, WS2005 1.34, average 1.64
- Prey Khmer: EWS2004 1.50, EWS2005 0.28, WS2004 1.94, WS2005 1.38, average 1.08
- O Rangeu: EWS2004 3.00, EWS2005 0.67, WS2004 1.86, WS2005 1.78, average 2.39
- Lveah Bansaek: EWS2004 4.50, EWS2005 n/a, WS2004 4.29, WS2005 n/a, average 4.40

Note on data quality: for most rows the printed "average" is close to the simple mean of the seasonal values shown, but for the Prey Khmer and O Rangeu rows the printed averages (1.08 and 2.39) are noticeably lower/different than a simple mean of their own four seasonal figures would give. This is reported as it appears in the source rather than corrected, since it isn't possible to tell from the document alone whether this reflects a different weighting method, missing data points, or a printing error.

Overall the results show large yield differences between soil groups -- from below 2 t/ha average on Prey Khmer and Kampong-Siem-with-lime soils, up to 4.4 t/ha average on Lveah Bansaek soil -- underlining that soil type is a major driver of corn yield potential in this region, independent of management.
